Bad Posture/ A Modern Disease

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at how our modern day work environment is setting us up for chronic pain

Unique Selling Point:
There is no doubt that tens of millions of people around the world continually suffer from bad posture as a result of the hours they spend slumped over their computers. In one report it was found that women between the ages of 35 and 50 who spend most of their time on social networking sites, 78% of them are in agony. 44% could not walk easily and 15% could not go out socially or to work. Curvature of the spine is causing havoc because it causes nerve damage, tightening muscles, weak core muscles etc. Carte Blanche investigates this and looks at modern trends to alleviate this fast growing medical phenomena. We ask are standing desks the way to go? Some experts say that whether you are sitting or standing for lengthy periods of time, it is the lack of movement that causes the issues.

We then look at proactive companies who are insisting that employees take a break from their desks every hour and even hold stand up meetings. We speak to an expert who will describe through nice 3d graphics exactly how our back become damages from inactivity and posture. We also drop in to a pain clinic to hear the devastating consequences of chronic back pain.

Its a semi-medical piece which will also describe non invasive procedures to alleviate symptoms and repair your posture. But it will be light as well as we look at some marvellous and eccentric designs that are on the market to encourage people to move away from their slumped positions.

Press Release:


Bad Posture: A Modern Disease
Could your office job be contributing to your risk of heart disease, obesity and early death? Carte Blanche finds out why sitting all day at our computers is seen as the new smoking, and why the trend of standing while working is taking off.


Script:


SCRIPT

Its a growing trend standing and working, with many people globally buying into the concept.

JP PROP24: Now that I am used to it, my back is feeling much much better.

Our sedentary lifestyles are taking their toll. Sitting in traffic for hours. Slouched at our computers the whole day, and taking these bad habits home are placing further stress on our necks. And as we pour over our devices, the consequences are far more serious than previously thought according to professor Vicki Lambert of the Sports Science Institute.

VICKI LAMBERT: We know for example and this has come even form the study of weightlessness in space because again there is no gravity and what have you that when you actually have prolonged sitting, it actually reduces the muscles ability to take up glucose for sugar, for energy. It also actually increases the fat in the blood of the triglycerides into the blood and it is also associated with an increase inflammatory profile and that is associated with chronic disease.

Sitting for extended hours with no exercise is referred to by some as the new smoking. Professor lambert alerted us to a Canadian researcher’s study

VICKI LAMBERT: When he queried people that sat for almost all of the time, the risk of dying of any cause was 50% greater. This has been replicated in studies in almost a quarter of a million adults in Australia and again most recently in a million adults in a combined cohort, globally.

And then there are the office injuries that some workers say they are picking up from extended hours sitting at their computers. Research psychologist Rebecca Hellman’s troubles began soon after leaving university and starting her first desk job.

REBECCA HELMAN: So the pain started in my shoulder but actually would sort of spread right up my neck and I would end up with really really bad headaches so it made it very difficult to work and just getting home every day in pain and then waking up feeling slightly better and knowing I was going to have to go back to a day of pain has been really difficult.

Prominent Cape Town Physiotherapist Lisa Radomsky is seeing the fall out.

JOHN: What percentage of people come through your door with office related complaints
LISA RADOMSKY: We probably find about 50% of some sort or other and you know even if they maybe not directly coming in with that, it certainly is a contributory factor. We see a broad spectrum of conditions but we see a lot of spinal conditions, a lot of back and neck problems, lower back problems, and a lot of it is because of poor ergonomics or people who just have jobs where they are sitting a lot in the day.

LINK: THE MODERN DAY LIFESTYLE AND WORK PLACE DEMANDS APPEAR TO HAVE LED TO AN EXPLOSION IN BACK AND NECK COMPLAINTS AND ITS THAT CONTEXT WHICH HAS GIVEN RISE TO A NEW BUZZWORD - OFFICE ERGONOMICS.

With the amount of research emerging, its no wonder some people are taking a serious look at their work spaces where they spend much of their day.

Cecily: People forget that they are walking biomechanics. You're a walking bunch of levers that interact very complexly in certain, and every time you move your arm, a whole lot of processes need to occur internally, externally, on so many different levels. But then you're interacting with a very static environment to some degree, and so ergonomics is finding a way to improve the external environment to accommodate the human being.

Cecily Schmidt, a physiotherapist by training now spends her time helping companies achieve a more ergonomic environment to avoid office injuries.

Cecily: So your common injuries are lower back pain, neck pain. I think the most common injury in office workers tends to be neck pain, tension in these muscles and over here, headaches and then arm pain. So a lot of people working particularly on the mouse tend to get pain here in the forearm and then carpal tunnel and that’s relating to a nerve here and they can get pins and needles, numbness and weakness in the hand.

But even the most ergonomic work station can't eliminate the impact of other factors such as age, smoking, stress and genetics.

Lisa: So for somebody that sits at their desk and does all the right things as far as exercise and posture is concerned but they really battle and then somebody else who has got absolutely shocking posture and never has a problem so there really isn’t a one size fits all.

But Schmidt says there are ways that we can improve our work station to help reduce the risk of developing pain. Unless you are visually impaired, she says that the screen should always be at arms length.

Cecily: And if it isn’t, you will tend to sit forward. So you can have a R12000 chair and not be using it because your monitor is sat at the wrong position and that is very very common.

She believes computer screens should always be at eye level to prevent your neck from bending and instead of buying a computer or monitor stand, two packs of printing paper will always do the trick.

An added element office ergonomics, are the standing desks which some say have reduced their office injuries as well as re-energizing them.

THEO: Sitting the whole day you are stuck and you are stuck in that position and just you and your screen where as when you are standing, you are a little bit more mobile, you see I’ve got my headphones on. I’m listening to music and occasionally then I do the little jiggle so its quite nice I’m able to move around a bit.

VICKI LAMBERT: Its not just about standing, and not just reducing sitting, its about reducing prolonged sitting time, its important to break up prolonged sitting time.

Professor Lambert believes that one should actually get up and walk about sixe times an hour but agrees this is impractical.

VICKY: The benefits for example of just getting up for a ten-minute period after 2-hour period of sitting are probably more practical and actually make more sense and the benefits are similar.

Some south African companies are now giving their workers the choice of whether to sit or stand while at work.

JP PROP24 CEO: I’ve found that ergonomics is very important to your productivity and your health and having found that out for myself you try and apply it to your work space for everyone else because you realize that if I was 20 years younger I would have wanted to know that and I would have wanted to work in an environment where my company had looked after us better.

A sedentary environment on the other hand could have a significant health impact says professor lambert.

VICKI LAMBERT: And so we know now that sitting time is an independent risk factor more many of these conditions, obesity cardiovascular disease, diabetes and even well all causes of mortality

With some research alerting us the to the perils of our sedentary lifestyles, legislation around ergonomics might soon be implemented in south Africa to reduce office injuries. A changing working environment is now almost certain.

Lisa: At the end of the day, prevention is better than cure. So it's all good and well to go to the physio or the chiropractor or the body stress release person, but you've got to be mindful about what you're doing during the day. And that would be about checking all the work surfaces and the things that you're doing that are going to prevent problems.
